themes.name: The Four Hinges
themes.note: The cardinal virtues, from Plato through Aristotle to Aquinas. Everything downstream hangs on one of these.

themes.name: The Three That Are Given
themes.note: Augustine and Aquinas treat these as received rather than achieved, which makes them sort differently from the rest.

themes.name: Seeing Clearly
themes.note: Aquinas breaks prudence into parts, and Aristotle names five intellectual virtues. Together they give a person a vocabulary for how they think.

themes.name: What I Owe
themes.note: Aquinas gathers a large family of virtues under justice, because each one names a debt.

themes.name: Standing Firm
themes.note: The parts of fortitude, which split cleanly into attacking and enduring.

themes.name: Largeness of Soul
themes.note: Aristotle's megalopsychia and megaloprepeia, which have no clean modern English and are worth reclaiming for owner-operators.

themes.name: Governing Myself
themes.note: The parts of temperance. Aquinas puts humility here, which surprises people and is worth surfacing in the room.

themes.name: The Restless Heart
themes.note: Augustinian interior life. These cards do the most work on the second half of the Identity question.

themes.name: Bound to Others
themes.note: Aristotle gives two full books of the Ethics to friendship, which earns this its own theme.

themes.name: Work and Craft
themes.note: Where the classical tradition meets the owner-operator, and where most of your participants live.

themes.name: Rest and Delight
themes.note: Josef Pieper's recovery of schole belongs here, and these cards tend to be the ones people are surprised to find themselves reaching for.

themes.name: The Things Worth Wanting
themes.note: Platonic transcendentals. These play differently from the rest, and they may serve better as the handoff into the Desire session's third pass than as sortable values.

cards.gloss: Governing my appetites so they serve what I love.

cards.gloss: Staying with what I have committed to.

cards.gloss: Doing the specific thing I said I would do.

cards.gloss: Acknowledging what came to me through someone else.

cards.gloss: Honoring family, place, and origin.

cards.gloss: Giving God, or the sacred, its due.

cards.gloss: Submitting to authority I have judged legitimate.

cards.gloss: Giving freely from what is mine.

cards.gloss: Treating ordinary people well in ordinary moments.

cards.gloss: Saying the unwelcome thing in the room where it matters.

cards.gloss: Staying with people when leaving would be easier.

cards.gloss: Giving up a real good for a greater one.

cards.gloss: Moving toward the risk on purpose.
cards.line: I move toward risk on purpose.

cards.gloss: Judging myself worthy of great things, and being right.

cards.gloss: Wanting more, for reasons that hold up.

cards.gloss: Beginning something before I am certain it will work.

cards.gloss: Keeping my life small enough to carry.
cards.line: I keep my life small enough to carry.

cards.gloss: Staying clear-headed.

cards.line: I decline to make myself the display.

cards.gloss: Holding an accurate estimate of myself.

cards.gloss: Keeping real strength under control.
cards.line: I keep real strength under control.

cards.gloss: Being satisfied with the portion I have.

cards.gloss: Playing and joking well. Aristotle counts this as a virtue, sitting between buffoonery and dourness.

cards.gloss: Taking real pleasure in what is good.
